passage:
"Ammi, can I have a laddoo?"
"One now," said Rehana, "or wait till after dinner and you get two."
Ojas stared at the steel box on the table. "Two is more."
"Yes."
"But dinner is so far."
"The rice will be ready when the cooker whistles three times."
Ojas sat on his hands. "One," he whispered at the first whistle. He turned his back to the box and hummed. "Two." He went to the balcony to watch the pigeons. "Three!"
After dinner he held out both palms. "You said two, Ammi."
"I did," said Rehana, and put two laddoos in them.

qa.q: How many whistles did the cooker need before the rice was ready?
qa.a: It needed three whistles.

qa.q: Why did Ojas sit on his hands and turn his back to the box?
qa.a: He was tempted but determined, stopping himself from grabbing a laddoo so that he could get two later.

qa.q: Why does it matter that Rehana kept her promise?
qa.a: Ojas learns that waiting really pays off and that he can trust her, so he is more likely to wait next time. 👍

qa.q: What would change if Rehana had forgotten and given only one?
qa.a: Ojas might feel tricked and decide it is better to grab things right away.

grounding: It shows a young child using simple tricks to resist a treat now in order to earn a bigger one later.

passage: Daycare note by Lavanya. Our children earn a paper token for each tidy-up. Three tokens buy a sticker; ten buy a turn with the big train set. Hemant, five, has seven tokens. Today he held them over the sticker tin for a long time, lips moving as he counted. Then he pushed them back into his pocket. "I'm saving for the train," he told me. He patted his pocket all afternoon. I will make a paper chart so he can colour a box for each token and see how close he is.

qa.q: How many tokens does Hemant have now?
qa.a: He has seven tokens.

qa.q: What does Hemant patting his pocket all afternoon suggest?
qa.a: He seems proud and a little tempted, keeping his tokens safe while he looks forward to the train set.

qa.q: How will Lavanya's chart help Hemant?
qa.a: Seeing his coloured boxes grow makes the waiting visible, so the later reward feels real and reachable.

qa.q: How might other children see Hemant not buying a sticker?
qa.a: Some may be puzzled, but seeing him get the train later could show them that waiting can bring a bigger prize.

grounding: It shows a five-year-old passing up a small reward now to save for a bigger one.

passage: In the hill village, the guava tree behind Lalremsiami's house hung heavy with hard green fruit. Tarun, six, reached for one. "Wait till they turn yellow," Lalremsiami said. "Then they're sweet, and Pi will give us a whole basket." Tarun's hand hung in the air. He picked up a stick instead and drew a guava in the mud. Each afternoon he checked: pressed one gently with his thumb, sniffed it, walked away. On the eighth day the fruit smelled sweet. Pi filled their basket, and Tarun ate three, juice running down his wrist.

qa.q: What colour did the guavas need to turn before picking?
qa.a: They needed to turn yellow.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when his hand hung near the green guava?
qa.a: He wanted to eat one right away but held back, trusting that waiting would bring sweet fruit and a whole basket.

qa.q: Why did drawing a guava in the mud help Tarun?
qa.a: It gave his hands and mind something else to do, which made it easier not to pick the fruit.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami see Tarun eating three sweet guavas?
qa.a: She may feel pleased that her advice paid off and that he trusted her.

grounding: It shows a young child resisting green fruit day after day to enjoy a bigger, sweeter reward later.

passage: On Wei's sixth birthday in Singapore, Aiko Ma had a plate of little cakes. 'You can eat one now, or wait until after dinner and have two.' Wei looked at the pink cake for a long time. He licked his lips. Then he pushed the plate away and went to play with his train, humming loudly. Twice he walked back and peeped. After dinner, Ma gave him two, and he beamed.

qa.q: What did Aiko Ma offer Wei if he waited until after dinner?
qa.a: She offered him two cakes.

qa.q: Why did Wei hum loudly while playing with his train?
qa.a: He felt tempted and impatient near the cake, so he hummed loudly to distract himself and keep waiting for the bigger reward.

qa.q: What strategy helped Wei wait, and what could he try next time?
qa.a: Pushing the plate away and playing elsewhere helped; next time he could ask for the plate to be put out of sight.

qa.q: How might Aiko Ma feel after keeping her promise?
qa.a: She may feel glad she kept her word, which helps Wei trust that waiting really pays off.

grounding: Illustrates a young child resisting an immediate temptation for a bigger delayed reward, in Singapore.

passage: In the school library corner, Chandrika Ma'am said, 'Anyone who wants can go to the sandpit now. Or stay for the whole story and get the first turn on the new swing.' Noor's friends ran out. Noor half stood up, looked at the door, then sat on her hands. She wriggled through the long story. When it ended, she ran first to the new swing and whooped as she flew.

qa.q: What reward did staying for the whole story bring?
qa.a: The first turn on the new swing.

qa.q: What does Noor sitting on her hands suggest about what she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt torn, wanting to run out with her friends but holding herself back to wait for the swing.

qa.q: What could Chandrika Ma'am say to Noor afterwards?
qa.a: She could notice how hard waiting was and name how Noor managed it, so Noor remembers what worked.

qa.q: How might Noor's friends feel when they see her get the first swing?
qa.a: They might feel a bit jealous and wish they had stayed, or decide to wait next time.

grounding: Shows a young child resisting an impulse to secure a larger delayed reward, in a school setting.

passage: I'm Anand, Zainab's older brother. On Sunday Ammi made jalebis. "Zainab, you can have one now, or two after lunch," she said. Zainab, who is five, stared at the plate. Then she sat on her hands and started singing loudly. She walked out of the kitchen and came back three times to look. I thought she'd grab one, but she waited. After lunch she ate both slowly, licking her fingers. I can't say what she was thinking, but she looked very pleased.

qa.q: What choice did Ammi give Zainab?
qa.a: One jalebi now, or two after lunch.

qa.q: Why might Zainab have sat on her hands and sung loudly?
qa.a: She was probably trying to resist the temptation, keeping busy so the wait felt easier.

qa.q: How could Ammi help Zainab build this skill?
qa.a: Praise her for waiting and keep her promise, so Zainab trusts that waiting pays off.

qa.q: How does Anand see Zainab's waiting?
qa.a: Anand expected her to grab one and is surprised she waited, though he can only guess what she thought.

grounding: Shows a young child resisting a treat now to get two later, seen by an older brother.

passage: Week one: Divyansh, five, picked a small green guava from Joseph Uncle's tree next door, bit it, and spat it out. Too sour. "Wait till they turn yellow," Joseph said, "they'll be sweet." Week two: Divyansh looked at the guavas every day. He touched one, then pulled his hand back. Week three: Joseph called him over. "Now." Divyansh picked a yellow guava and bit it. "Sweet!" he said. "I waited so long!"

qa.q: What happened when Divyansh bit the green guava?
qa.a: It was too sour, and he spat it out.

qa.q: What does Divyansh pulling his hand back in week two suggest?
qa.a: He was tempted but chose to wait because he trusted Joseph that the guavas would be sweet later.

qa.q: How did Joseph help Divyansh learn to wait?
qa.a: He explained what waiting would bring and called him when the fruit was ready, so the promise came true.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel when Divyansh says "Sweet!"?
qa.a: Pleased and warm, seeing the boy enjoy the reward of his patience.

grounding: Shows a young child learning over three weeks to resist picking fruit early for a sweeter reward.

passage: It was raining hard, and Lokesh, six, had just been given a new kite. "Let's open it now!" he said. His older brother Chinmay shook his head. "If we open it inside, it'll tear. If we wait till tomorrow, we can fly it on the roof." Lokesh groaned and pressed his nose to the window. He hugged the kite in its plastic, then put it on the top shelf where he couldn't see it. The next morning, the sky was clear.

qa.q: What did Chinmay say would happen if they opened the kite inside?
qa.a: If they open it inside, it'll tear.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh put the kite on the top shelf?
qa.a: He was impatient and tempted to open it, so hiding it helped him wait.

qa.q: What did Chinmay do that helped Lokesh wait?
qa.a: He explained the reason and the bigger reward of flying it tomorrow.

qa.q: What would change if Lokesh had opened it inside?
qa.a: The kite might have torn and he'd have lost the chance to fly it the next day.

grounding: Shows a young child waiting out a rainy day rather than opening a new kite indoors, to fly it properly later.

passage: The sweet shop in Lajpat Nagar smelled of hot sugar. Parveen, five, pressed her nose to the glass. "One jalebi now," said Irawati Khala, "or two after dinner if you wait. Your choice." Parveen looked at the orange spirals for a long time. "Two," she said. Then she turned her back to the counter and hummed loudly all the way home. At dinner she ate fast and asked, "Now?" Khala laughed and put two jalebis on her plate.

qa.q: What choice did Irawati Khala give Parveen?
qa.a: One jalebi now, or two after dinner if she waited.

qa.q: Why did Parveen turn her back to the counter and hum loudly?
qa.a: She was tempted by the jalebis and was keeping herself from looking at them so she could wait for two.

qa.q: What did Irawati Khala do that made it easier for Parveen to wait?
qa.a: She made the choice clear and let Parveen choose, then kept her word after dinner.

qa.q: What would change if Irawati Khala had forgotten her promise at dinner?
qa.a: Parveen would likely feel let down and be less willing to wait next time.

grounding: A five-year-old turns away and hums to resist one jalebi now for two after dinner.

passage:
On Diwali evening, Aadhya held the box of phuljhadis.
"Mumma, light one now! Please!"
"It's still light out," said Himani. "If you wait till it's dark and Papa is home, we can light four together."
"Four?"
"Four. But not one now."
Aadhya put the box on the table. She picked it up. She put it down again. "I'll count the diyas," she said, and walked away from the box to count.
Later, in the dark, she held the fourth sparkler high. "It was worth it!"

qa.q: How many sparklers did Himani promise if Aadhya waited?
qa.a: Four, once it was dark and Papa was home.

qa.q: What does Aadhya picking up the box and putting it down again suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt a strong pull to light one right away and was struggling to wait.

qa.q: Which strategy helped Aadhya wait?
qa.a: She moved away from the box and busied herself counting diyas.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt when Aadhya said, "It was worth it"?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and glad that her daughter managed to wait. 🙂

grounding: A young girl distracts herself on Diwali to wait for four sparklers instead of one straight away.

passage: Class KG-B, Christmas party, 20 December. Note by Kavitha, class teacher. I offered each child a slice of plum cake now, or a whole small cake to decorate and take home after the carol practice. Jeevan chose to wait. During practice he kept looking at the cake tray, then deliberately sat facing the window. Twice he said, "I'm waiting, I'm waiting," to himself. When practice ended he was first to the table and spent a long time with the icing. I told his father at pickup, and I'll give him the tray-carrying job tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Jeevan do during practice to keep from looking at the tray?
qa.a: He deliberately sat facing the window.

qa.q: What does Jeevan saying "I'm waiting, I'm waiting" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt tempted and was reminding himself of his goal to stay patient.

qa.q: What did Kavitha do after noticing Jeevan's effort?
qa.a: She told his father at pickup and planned to give him the tray-carrying job.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's father feel hearing about the plum cake?
qa.a: He would likely feel proud that his son chose to wait for the bigger reward.

grounding: A teacher's note records a kindergartner waiting through carol practice for a cake to decorate instead of a slice now.

passage:
On Christmas morning in the village near Margao, Maria, five, saw the bebinca on the table.

"One piece now, or two after church," Naveen Uncle said.

Maria stared at the cake. She sat on her hands and sang all the carols she knew, very loudly. She didn't look at the table.

After church, she ran home first. "I waited! Two pieces!"

qa.q: What did Naveen Uncle offer if Maria waited?
qa.a: He offered two pieces after church.

qa.q: How did Maria feel while she waited?
qa.a: Maria felt tempted and impatient, but determined to get the bigger reward.

qa.q: What strategies helped Maria wait?
qa.a: She sat on her hands, sang loudly, and didn't look at the table.

qa.q: How might Naveen Uncle feel when Maria came back?
qa.a: Naveen Uncle was probably amused and proud of her patience.

grounding: On Christmas morning, a child resists eating cake straight away to earn a larger reward later.

passage:
On the eve of Three Kings' Day in Barcelona, Rosa, five, found a wrapped present under the bed.

"Don't open it till morning," said her sister Layla. "If you wait, the kings will bring the second one too."

Rosa sat on the floor staring at it. Layla gave her a book. "Read to me instead."

Rosa read, then drew pictures, then fell asleep. In the morning, there were two presents.

qa.q: Where did Rosa find the present?
qa.a: She found a wrapped present under the bed.

qa.q: How did Rosa feel staring at the present?
qa.a: Rosa felt tempted and excited, finding it hard to wait.

qa.q: How did Layla help Rosa wait?
qa.a: Layla gave her something else to do, like reading and drawing, so the present was out of her mind.

qa.q: How might Layla feel in the morning?
qa.a: Layla would likely feel pleased that Rosa waited.

grounding: On the eve of Three Kings' Day, a child resists opening a present to get a larger reward in the morning.

passage:
It was Children's Day at the preschool. Hrithik Sir held up a sticker sheet.

"One sticker now, or two if you tidy the blocks first."

Charu wanted the shiny star now. Her hand reached out. Then she pulled it back.

She tidied the blocks as fast as she could, counting them out loud to help. Then she held out her hand. "Two, please."

qa.q: How many stickers did Charu get for tidying first?
qa.a: She asked for two stickers.

qa.q: How did Charu feel when she reached for the sticker?
qa.a: Charu felt tempted and eager, wanting the shiny star straight away.

qa.q: What helped Charu wait for the bigger reward?
qa.a: She pulled her hand back, kept busy tidying and counted out loud.

qa.q: How might Hrithik Sir feel when Charu chose to wait?
qa.a: Hrithik Sir was likely pleased and proud of her self-control.

grounding: On Children's Day, a child resists taking a sticker straight away to earn two after tidying up.

passage: I'm Jomon, Farida's neighbour. During Ramzan I often go over at sunset. Yesterday her Nani put out jalebis and told Farida, "One now, or three after we break the fast." Farida stared at the plate. Then she sat on her hands, turned her back to it and started singing loudly. Her cousin Sameer ate one and waved it at her. She shut her eyes. When the call to prayer sounded and everyone broke the fast, she got her three. I don't know how she did it; I'd have grabbed one.

qa.q: What did Nani offer Farida?
qa.a: One jalebi now, or three after they break the fast.

qa.q: Why did Farida sit on her hands and turn her back to the plate?
qa.a: She was tempted by the jalebis but wanted the three later, so she felt determined to keep herself from grabbing one.

qa.q: How could Farida's family encourage this waiting in other situations?
qa.a: They could keep promises as Nani did, so Farida trusts that waiting really brings the bigger reward.

qa.q: How does Jomon see Farida's waiting?
qa.a: Jomon is impressed, admitting that grabbing one would have been hard to resist.

grounding: Illustrates a young child resisting a sweet now so she can have more later, seen by a neighbour.
